name: New York
note: AFL-CIO president John Sweeney, whose mother had worked as a domestic worker for over forty years, traveled to Albany to lobby personally for the bill. His testimony was credited as a turning point in the campaign's final push.

name: Hawaii
note: The bill passed both chambers with little opposition and took effect the same day it was signed, one of the fastest implementation timelines of any domestic workers law in the country.

name: California
note: California is the only state to pass two separate pieces of domestic worker legislation, the original 2013 law and another in 2016, which made it permanent. No other state has returned to strengthen its law through a second bill.

name: Massachusetts
note: The law guaranteed eight weeks of unpaid parental leave to domestic workers employed by the same household for at least three months, and required employers to pay workers for all time they were required to be on the premises, including before and after scheduled shifts.

name: Connecticut
note: The bill drew near-unanimous support across both chambers, with bipartisan votes that produced some of the broadest legislative margins of any domestic workers law passed to date.

name: Oregon
note: Governor Kate Brown, who signed the bill in her first year in office, was the first openly bisexual governor in United States history, having assumed office in February 2015 following her predecessor's resignation.

name: Illinois
note: The five-year campaign was led by the Illinois Domestic Workers Coalition, a multiethnic organizing effort drawing workers from Latino, Filipino, and Polish communities across Chicago and the state.

name: Nevada
note: The bill passed the Senate on a strict party-line vote with all Republicans opposed. Governor Brian Sandoval, a Republican widely noted as a moderate, signed it anyway, one of only two Republican governors to sign a domestic workers law.

name: Seattle
note: The ordinance established the first Domestic Worker Standards Board of any city in the country, creating a formal body to investigate industry conditions and make ongoing recommendations on worker health, safety, and wellbeing.

name: New Mexico
note: Signed during Governor Lujan Grisham's first year in office, it extended minimum wage protections to domestic workers for the first time in the state's history, bringing New Mexico into alignment with the growing majority of states that had already acted.

name: Philadelphia
note: The law introduced the first portable paid leave system of any domestic workers ordinance: workers accrue paid time off across multiple employers, with each employer contributing a pro-rated share based on hours worked.

name: Virginia
note: Senator Jennifer McClellan, who sponsored the bill, described her family's multigenerational history in domestic work as the direct personal background behind her commitment to the legislation. Her great-grandmother, grandmother, and mother had all worked as domestic workers.

name: District of Columbia
note: It was the first domestic workers law to undergo congressional review before taking effect, as required under the District Clause of the Constitution. The DC Council voted unanimously to pass it.

name: New Jersey
note: Murphy signed the bill as part of a package of three immigrants' rights laws on the same day, one of the broader single-day legislative signings on labor and immigration in the state's recent history.

name: Rhode Island
note: The law took effect immediately upon signing, with no implementation delay. It worked by removing a single statutory provision that had explicitly classified domestic workers as non-employees under Rhode Island's minimum wage law.

name: Washington
note: Representative Brianna Thomas, the bill's prime sponsor, cleaned houses with her mother as a child in Georgia. She carried that experience to Olympia, where the bill passed after years of coalition building across the state.
